analysis.one_liner: Strips ocean shipping lines of their exemption from federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Ocean shipping lines are currently exempt from federal antitrust laws, meaning they can coordinate on rates and capacity without facing lawsuits for anti-competitive behavior. This bill would repeal that exemption, expose carriers to normal antitrust enforcement, and let the Federal Maritime Commission formally weigh in on mergers between shipping companies reviewed by the Justice Department. The idea is that more competition in ocean freight would lower shipping costs, which are passed on to American exporters, importers, and shoppers.
analysis.who_benefits: American farmers and manufacturers who export goods overseas, retailers and other importers who pay freight charges, and ultimately consumers, since shipping costs are baked into the price of goods. Antitrust exposure would also give shippers a legal tool against carriers that coordinate to keep rates or capacity tight.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the section of federal maritime law (46 U.S.C. 40307) that exempts ocean common carriers from federal antitrust laws, so carriers can be sued and prosecuted like other industries for anti-competitive conduct.
Preserves a narrower exemption only for agreements about collectively bargained fringe benefit obligations, keeping labor-related arrangements intact while ending rate-and-capacity immunity.

Authorizes the Federal Maritime Commission to analyze and submit written views to the Justice Department's Antitrust Division on mergers and acquisitions involving shipping carriers and marine terminal operators, and to report to Congress on competition impacts.

analysis.who_pays: Foreign and domestic ocean shipping lines and marine terminal operators, which lose their immunity from antitrust suits and face possible challenges to the rate-setting and capacity coordination they do through alliances. The bill's backers argue those costs are the point of antitrust enforcement; carriers argue coordination is essential to running efficient scheduled services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ocean shipping lines and their alliances

drawbacks.text: Carriers and some trade groups argue the antitrust exemption lets shipping lines form alliances that coordinate schedules and share vessel capacity, which keeps service reliable on routes too thin to support many independent competitors; removing it could reduce efficiency and raise the cost of operating global shipping networks.

The timing argument: global freight rates spiked to record levels during the 2021-2022 supply chain crunch but had largely normalized by the time this bill was introduced, weakening the urgency that motivated similar legislation during the pandemic.

The bill leaves antitrust review of shipping mergers primarily with the Justice Department, adding an advisory role for the Maritime Commission rather than giving a maritime-specific regulator direct enforcement power over consolidation in the industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to a broad, diffuse group — anyone who buys imported goods or exports products — in the form of lower freight costs and legal recourse against coordinated conduct by a handful of giant carriers. The cost falls on a concentrated industry that profits from immunity, and the strongest counterargument is that immunity also enables operational efficiencies through alliances. Congress never weighed these tradeoffs, because the bill never received any committee or floor action.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary and Transportation committees in March 2023 and to a Transportation subcommittee the next day, and neither panel ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Jim Costa introduced the bill on March 22, 2023 with four original cosponsors: Reps. Garamendi, Panetta, and Harder (D-CA) and Dusty Johnson (R-SD).
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and, for provisions in its jurisdiction, to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
The next day it was referred to the Transportation and Infrastructure Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation.
No committee vote, markup, report, or floor action ever occurred, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Ocean shipping carriers kept their antitrust exemption and their ability to coordinate rates and capacity without antitrust exposure. Shippers and consumers gained nothing; the status quo that produced record freight rates during the supply chain crisis remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ocean carriers keep their antitrust exemption

for.name: Jim Costa
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to repeal the ocean shipping antitrust exemption.

for.name: Garamendi, Panetta, Harder, and Johnson of South Dakota
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a small bipartisan base.

against.name: House Judiciary and Transportation and Infrastructure Committees
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in the 22 months between referral and the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote to measure, and support was nominally bipartisan — three Democrats and one Republican cosponsored — but no action ever followed referral.

industries.industry: Ocean common carriers and shipping alliances
industries.note: These carriers — a handful of large foreign and domestic lines operating through alliances — hold an antitrust exemption that lets them coordinate on rates and capacity without antitrust suits. The bill repeals that shield, so the industry's interest in killing the bill runs directly against shippers' and consumers' interest in lower freight costs and competition.

The bill subjects marine terminal operators to the same antitrust exposure as carriers, since the FERC-style merger comment provision covers them too and the repeal targets the carrier exemption regime they operate under.

Exporters of farm goods and manufactured products pay ocean freight to reach foreign customers; when carriers face antitrust exposure, exporters gain a legal tool against coordinated rate and capacity conduct that squeezed them during the pandemic freight spike.
Importers bore record ocean freight costs during 2021-2022 that were passed into consumer prices; antitrust exposure for carriers raises the prospect of more competition and lower shipping charges.
